title: If people knew
hook: if beings knew the fruit of giving, they would not eat without sharing (Itivuttaka 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, glad three times: glad before giving, bright while giving, uplifted after. Your line was glad three times. Did you catch all three moments once? Day one hundred thirty-four.

Picture the last slice of pizza in the box. Four people around the table. Everybody saw it. Nobody's reaching. There's a tiny standoff that every family, every office, every group of roommates knows. Someone finally says, go on, split it? Now picture the same slice when you're alone at midnight, and it's simply gone, no thought at all. The Buddha said something about that last bite, a line so strong that it can sound almost impossible. It's in a small book of his sayings, and it begins with three words: if people knew.
screen: `THE LAST SLICE IN THE BOX.` → `A TINY STANDOFF.` → `IF PEOPLE KNEW.`

segments.voice: The book is the Itivuttaka, which means this was said, a collection of short teachings the tradition remembers as the Buddha's own words. In saying twenty-six, he says, in substance: if beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, they would not eat without first giving. The stain of stinginess would not take hold of their minds. Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat it without sharing, if there were someone to share it with. But because they don't know, he says, they eat without giving, and stinginess stains their minds. Notice what this teaching is, and what it isn't. It isn't a command: thou shalt share. It's a claim about knowledge. The problem isn't that people are bad. It's that they don't see what giving actually does. If they could see it, sharing would be as obvious as stepping out of the rain. What does giving do? The texts talk about good results in this life and future lives. But they also point to something you can check tonight. Stinginess is a stain, and it's a tight, small feeling. Sharing loosens it. Think of the last slice again. When someone finally splits it, the whole table relaxes. Nobody got much pizza. Everybody got something better. And look at the word the saying uses: the last bite. Not the leftovers, not what you didn't want. Sharing the last of something is where generosity stops being easy and starts being real.
screen: `ITIVUTTAKA: THIS WAS SAID.` · `IF THEY KNEW THE FRUIT OF GIVING.` · `NOT A COMMAND, A WAY OF SEEING.` · `STINGINESS IS A STAIN.` · then, large: `SHARE THE LAST BITE.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Think of something you usually keep to yourself: the last cookie, the good seat, the end of the coffee, an hour of quiet. Notice the little tightness when you imagine giving it away. Don't fight it; just feel where it sits in the body. Then picture yourself sharing it anyway, and the other person's surprise. Notice what happens to the tightness. Breathe with whatever you find. The bell holds the time.
If people knew. The Buddha's saying that if beings knew the fruit of giving, they wouldn't eat even their last bite without sharing.
Your line: share the last bite. Today, share part of a meal: half a sandwich, the last slice, a coffee for the person next to you. Day one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists set aside part of a meal to offer first, at a home shrine, to monks or to guests, and sharing food is one of the most common everyday forms of dana.

myth: the saying is a command: thou shalt share
it's a claim about knowing: if beings knew the fruit of giving, they would share.
the saying mentions even the last bite, the last mouthful
even then, they would not eat without sharing, if someone were there.
the Itivuttaka's name means 'this was said'
it's a collection of short sayings remembered as the Buddha's own.

fork.setup: according to the saying, why do people eat without sharing?
options: because they don't know the fruit of giving.
fork.reveal: the saying puts it down to not knowing: if they saw what giving does, sharing would be obvious.

original.note: Pali: sharing, dividing out; the saying speaks of giving and sharing (dana-samvibhaga).

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule that good people share.
what it means: a claim about seeing clearly; if we knew what giving does, we couldn't help sharing.
what a scholar hears: Itivuttaka 26 pairs dana with samvibhaga, sharing, and calls stinginess (macchera) a stain (mala) on the mind.

notes: Itivuttaka 26 is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm that the paraphrase ('if beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing… even their last morsel, last mouthful') is faithful.
The Pali terms samvibhaga, macchera and mala in the trapdoor should be checked against the text.
